script.title: Why Everything Depends on One Factory

sections.label: COLD OPEN
sections.text: The most advanced chips in the world — the ones inside every AI model, every smartphone, every cloud server, every weapons system — all come from one company. One factory. One island. There is no backup. That is not a simplification. It is the literal structure of the most critical supply chain in the global economy. And almost nobody who depends on it actually understands how it works.
sections.speaker_directions: Direct, controlled. Opening line delivered slowly — one clause at a time. No warmth. Quiet authority. Pace builds slightly toward the final sentence.

enhancement_cues.description: Near-black screen. Bone text appears one clause at a time: 'One company. One factory. One island.' Each phrase appears, holds 1.5s, then the next arrives. No diagram yet.

sections.label: THE SURFACE STORY
sections.text:
Most people think they understand where chips come from. Apple designs Apple chips. NVIDIA designs NVIDIA chips. Samsung, AMD, Qualcomm, Broadcom — each company appears to have its own silicon. You watch the keynotes. You read the product names. The story holds together convincingly.

It is not how any of it works.

Every one of those companies is what the industry calls fabless. They design chips. They do not manufacture them. Chip design is intellectual work — writing logic, architecting transistors, optimizing circuits. It happens on computers in California, Texas, and Taipei. Chip manufacturing is something entirely different.

Building a leading-edge chip requires machines that print circuits using extreme ultraviolet light — wavelengths shorter than the diameter of a virus. A single modern leading-edge fab costs over twenty billion dollars to construct. The equipment takes years to install and qualify. And the process expertise — the yield knowledge, the defect reduction data, the process integration — takes decades of continuous production to accumulate. That knowledge does not live in a patent or a blueprint. It lives in the team and in the data.

Fabless companies cannot build this. So they all go to the same place.
sections.speaker_directions: First paragraph: measured, slightly ironic. 'It is not how any of it works.' — flat, dry, delivered as a statement not a gotcha. Second paragraph onward: explanatory, building.

sections.label: THE ACTUAL SYSTEM
sections.text:
That place is a foundry — a factory that manufactures chips on behalf of design companies without designing them itself. The foundry model was invented in 1987 by an engineer named Morris Chang, who understood that design and manufacturing could be cleanly separated. Fabless companies could optimize for design. Foundries could optimize for manufacturing. Each side could specialize at scale.

It worked completely. Today, nearly every advanced chip on earth flows through this structure.

The supply chain runs through five layers.

At the top: EDA software. Electronic design automation — tools built primarily by American companies — gives engineers the ability to design chips containing billions of transistors. U.S. firms capture more than forty percent of global chip design market share, including the EDA tools that make the entire chain possible. Without EDA, advanced chip design at nanometer scales cannot happen anywhere.

Below that: fabless design houses. Apple, NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Broadcom, and hundreds of others translate circuit ideas into the precise manufacturing files a fab needs to build the chip. This is intellectual work. It produces no physical object.

Below that: the foundry. The factory where chips are physically made. Silicon wafers are grown, circuits are printed through lithography using machines that cost a hundred and fifty million dollars each, and transistors are formed at atomic precision. This is the third layer. This is where the system narrows.

Below that: OSAT — outsourced semiconductor assembly and test. After fabrication, chips are packaged, interconnected, and tested for function. Most OSAT capacity sits in Taiwan, South Korea, and Southeast Asia — another geographic concentration inside the chain.

At the bottom: OEM assembly. Device manufacturers integrate everything into the phones, servers, vehicles, and infrastructure that the world runs on.

Five layers. Work distributed across three continents. Hundreds of billions of dollars in annual investment. And the entire chain connects through one company in the third layer.
sections.speaker_directions: Explanatory and building. The five-layer list should be delivered with slight weight on each 'below that' — each is a reveal. Pace slows at 'This is where the system narrows.'

sections.label: THE CHOKEPOINT
sections.text:
That company is TSMC. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. Founded in 1987 — the same year the foundry model was invented, by the same man who invented it. Headquartered in Hsinchu, Taiwan. Approximately sixty thousand employees. Annual revenue near one hundred twenty-five billion dollars in 2025.

TSMC does not design chips. It does not sell chips. It only manufactures. And it manufactures at a scale and precision that no other company on earth currently matches.

At the most advanced process nodes — the three-nanometer and two-nanometer processes that power the fastest AI accelerators, the most capable phones, and the highest-performance processors — industry analysts estimate TSMC's market share is above ninety percent. Samsung holds about twelve percent of the overall foundry market. Intel is attempting to re-enter foundry manufacturing after years of delays. But at leading-edge nodes, at volume, today, there is no viable alternative. The tree of substitutes is empty.

The gap is not just about capacity. It is about yield. When a fab runs a process, not every chip works. The fraction that functions correctly is called yield. Yield determines whether a business is viable. Industry analysts report TSMC's yield at the two-nanometer node at approximately sixty-five to seventy percent. Samsung's competing two-nanometer process started at roughly thirty percent in early 2025 test runs, and industry tracking firms report it has improved to an estimated fifty to sixty percent by late 2025. Intel's 18A process carries reported yields in the fifty-five to sixty-five percent range — but it is not available to fabless customers. Intel is producing 18A for its own internal chip programs only. The yield gap remains consequential. At leading-edge volume, available to external customers today, TSMC has no credible substitute.

The demand concentrated at TSMC is now being driven primarily by artificial intelligence. Analysts project NVIDIA will displace Apple as TSMC's largest single customer in 2026 — the first time in the company's history that AI accelerator orders outpace consumer device demand at the world's most advanced fab. TSMC's first-quarter 2026 revenue reached thirty-five point nine billion dollars — forty point six percent year-on-year growth in U.S. dollar terms — a new quarterly record. The chokepoint is not weakening under this pressure. It is strengthening.
sections.speaker_directions: Open with the name slowly and cleanly — 'TSMC. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company.' Then build through the market share stats with increasing weight. The yield comparison should be delivered matter-of-factly — the numbers speak. Final sentence: deliberate, conclusive.

sections.label: WHO BENEFITS
sections.text:
Here is the structural layer that most analysis misses.

You cannot simply build another TSMC. This is not a claim about political will or capital availability. The United States has committed fifty-two billion dollars through the CHIPS Act to rebuild domestic semiconductor manufacturing. The European Union has pledged forty-three billion euros through its own Chips Act. Japan has committed the equivalent of over twenty-five billion dollars in semiconductor subsidies. Every government that depends on advanced chips — which is every major government — has looked at this concentration and concluded it is a strategic liability.

TSMC is building a fabrication plant in Arizona. It is operational. It is producing chips there. But the Arizona facility is running on the N4 process node — two full generations behind TSMC's most advanced production in Taiwan. N3 production at the Arizona facility is not expected until 2027 at the earliest. N2 has no confirmed date. At current ramp rates, the Arizona investment will not materially change the global dependency picture before 2028.

Morris Chang — the man who invented the foundry model, the founder of TSMC — stated publicly that the effort to replicate TSMC in the United States is, in his words, a very expensive exercise in futility.

His reasoning is not about technology or capital. It is about ecosystem. In Taiwan, every supplier, equipment specialist, process engineer, and material vendor that TSMC depends on is within an hour of the fabrication facility. Chemical suppliers. Tool maintenance engineers. Lithography specialists. Wafer material vendors. Equipment calibration technicians. Hundreds of companies, thousands of workers, all optimized over decades to support one integrated production environment. That proximity took thirty years to develop through co-location, iteration, and shared institutional learning across an entire regional economy. It cannot be packaged and shipped. The knowledge is in the relationships, the proximity, and the accumulated production data. You cannot fly the ecosystem to Arizona. You can only grow another one — and that takes time measured in decades, not appropriations cycles.

The Arizona fab is real. The investment is real. The intent is real. The timeline is honest: structural dependency on Taiwan will not end this decade.
sections.speaker_directions: Open flatly: 'Here is the structural layer that most analysis misses.' Not dramatic — just direct. The Morris Chang quote should be delivered as a direct quotation, slight weight on 'his words'. Final three sentences: short, declarative, each on its own beat.

sections.label: THE LEVERAGE MAP
sections.text:
So where exactly is the leverage?

TSMC holds pricing power, schedule power, and strategic weight that is entirely disproportionate to the size of any single customer or government. That leverage does not require active extraction. It does not require toll booths or platform rules. It is the structural consequence of irreplaceability. When a system depends on a single node that cannot be bypassed or substituted, that node holds leverage by existing.

Inside the primary chokepoint, there is a second one.

TSMC's CoWoS technology — chip-on-wafer-on-substrate — is the advanced packaging process that physically connects AI accelerator chips to the high-bandwidth memory they require to function. Every major AI training system in production today relies on this packaging. Without CoWoS, a competitive AI accelerator cannot be built at commercial scale.

TSMC's CoWoS capacity is sold out through 2026. Demand is growing faster than TSMC can expand capacity. Projected output is rising from thirty-five thousand wafers per month in 2024 to targeting around one hundred thirty thousand by end-2026 — a near-fourfold increase in two years — and it will still be insufficient to meet demand. NVIDIA alone is expected to consume more than half of all CoWoS output.

The implication is direct: the supply of AI compute is not governed by capital availability, by the number of companies building hardware, by regulatory conditions, or by geopolitical pressure. It is governed by the production schedule of one factory and the available capacity of one packaging process. Both are in Taiwan. Both are controlled by the same company.

This is a chokepoint inside a chokepoint. The system narrows twice before reaching the product.

The CoWoS section should accelerate slightly — it's the reveal within the reveal. Final line: slow, conclusive, deliberate.

sections.label: STRATEGIC TAKEAWAY
sections.text:
The model here is reusable.

TSMC is not a unique accident. The world contains dozens of systems that appear, from the outside, to be competitive markets — but are, on careful examination, single-node dependencies. The test is the same in every case: can the system function at the required quality level if this node is removed or constrained? If the answer is no, the node is a chokepoint. Not a competitive advantage. A structural gate.

Finding these gates requires following dependencies upstream. Follow the supply chain past the branded layer. Ignore the logos. Ask what each layer actually depends on to function. Ask it again for each dependency. At what point does the tree stop branching? At what point do all paths converge? Where does the system narrow to one entity with no adequate substitute?

At TSMC, it narrows to one at the third layer of a five-layer chain, in a country that three major powers have each independently assessed as the most geopolitically exposed piece of real estate in the world. The United States, China, and Taiwan have all reached this conclusion separately. The governments that understood the exposure earliest have spent the most capital the fastest — and still cannot close the gap within this decade.

The leverage map looks like this: one node, ninety percent market share, no adequate alternative, timeline measured in years not months, pricing power that compounds as AI demand increases. Every actor in the system is exposed. The actor who controls the node does not need to do anything aggressive to exercise that leverage. It simply needs to keep running.

If you want to understand where power concentrates in AI hardware — not where it appears to concentrate, but where the system literally cannot function without a specific node — TSMC is the clearest example available right now.

The research stack I use for this kind of mapping is linked in the description.
sections.speaker_directions: Open with 'The model here is reusable' — flat, like the start of a conclusion. Second paragraph: methodical, teaching. The 'leverage map looks like this' section: each clause lands as its own beat, slightly slower. Final two sentences: authoritative close, no sentimental warmth.
